item.title: You Can Ditch Postman Now, A Practical Guide to the API Testing Tool Bruno (Part 2) - Advanced
item.description:
In the previous articles 【】 and 【】, we introduced the pros and cons and the basic usage of Bruno, the API testing tool that has recently attracted much attention. In this article, building on the previous one, we will continue by introducing the advanced usage of Bruno related to test automation.

Bruno’s Six Levels of Variable Scope

Similar to Postman, Bruno also provides a multi-layered design for the use of variables in API testing, distinguished by scopes at different levels, which brings more flexibility and application scenarios to API testing and automation.

Bruno offers 6 different types of variables, and the order of their scopes is as follows:

Global Variables

Global variables are the variable type with the widest scope. Global variables are set through Bruno’s global Environments settings, located as follows:

Then, for example, add a global variable, configure it, and enable it:

At this point we fetch user information from the Github API, and can retrieve the user with userid = 1.

Collection Variables

After setting global variables, then set collection variables.

Then send the request - what takes effect now is the collection variable.

Environment Variables

The next level lets you configure different environments, set up in the following location:

What takes effect now is userid = 3.

Folder Variables

One level below the collection, you can create folders; setting variables here makes them folder variables that take effect.

Request Variables

One level further down are the variables set within a specific request.

Runtime Variables

Beyond preset variables, Bruno also supports setting runtime variables at execution time through scripts, using the following code:

1

bru.setVar("userid", 6)

After executing the request, to view the current runtime variables you can also open the display view via the corresponding button in the toolbar.

From the examples above, you can see Bruno’s multi-level variable system and its scopes. For the same variable name, the order of precedence is as follows:

Runtime Variables -> Request Variables -> Folder Variables -> Environment Variables -> Collection Variables -> Global Variables

Process Environment Variables

Beyond these multi-level variable designs, when working with APIs, sensitive data variables such as tokens, API Keys, or certain account passwords may be things we do not want to appear in the API and its related configuration files ( *.bru ). For this type of variable, Bruno also provides a targeted solution, namely storing them through a .env file. The .env file needs to be placed in the root directory of the collection, and variables are defined in key-value form, for example:

1

userid = 7

At this point, when configuring variables we can reference them via {{process.env.userid}}, avoiding sensitive data appearing directly in the API definition files.

Bruno Scripts and Execution Order

Bruno’s scripting feature uses standard JavaScript syntax. You can define scripts to be executed before (Pre) and after (Post) a request at three different levels: Collection, Folder, and Request. Bruno also provides two script execution order models (the main difference being the execution order of post scripts).

1. Sandwich Flow (Default)

In this mode, the execution order of scripts at different levels is as follows.

  • Collection Pre Script
    • Folder Pre Script
      • Request Pre Script
  • Request Post Script
    • Folder Post Script
      • Collection Post Script

This is similar to the layered execution order of various unit testing frameworks.

2. Sequential (Natural) Flow

This execution order is similar to Postman’s script execution order, following the hierarchy strictly level by level.

  • Collection Pre Script
    • Folder Pre Script
      • Request Pre Script
  • Collection Post Script
    • Folder Post Script
      • Request Post Script

To adopt this order, you need to configure the flow parameter in Bruno’s configuration file bruno.json, in a form like:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
9


{
 "scripts": {
 "filesystemAccess": {
 "allow": true
 },
 "flow": "sequential" // Or "sandwich"
 }
}

Execution Example

Add corresponding script logs to the scripts at each level, open Bruno’s integrated Dev Tool console, and you can see the difference in execution order.

Modify bruno.json and set the flow mode to sequential, and you can see that the output order of the post portion changes.

Handling Flow Dependencies

In real API testing, a frequently encountered scenario is that a later request depends on the response data of an earlier request, such as the most common case of obtaining a dynamic token.

Using Bruno’s variables and scripts, we can implement this kind of request correlation through scripts.

In Bruno’s official documentation, its built-in bru object provides methods such as setNextRequest and runRequest, allowing us, as needed, to specify the next request to execute when running a given API request (instead of following the default order), or to directly run other API requests from within the current request’s script.

In this way, by setting variables and passing them between APIs, we can implement flow dependency scenarios.

For example, here we fetch the list of repos under a github user via this API. Here we want the {{username}} variable to be obtained by specifying a userid. That is, first execute the earlier getUserInfo API and, based on userid, obtain username.

Here we define getUserRepos using the variable {{username}}, but at this point the variable is undefined, so it is shown in red.

Then in the getUserInfo API, we define a script that extracts the username from the current response and assigns it to a variable, then directly calls the getUserRepos API (note that the API path called here should be defined relative to the collection root path).

1
2
3
4
5
6


bru.setVar("username",res.body.login)

const response = await bru.runRequest("variables/getUserRepos")

console.log(response.status)

Execute getUserInfo and you can see it succeeds; the getUserRepos API executed in the script also successfully gets a 200OK response status.

Runner

Besides running a specified API in a script, Bruno also provides a Runner executor. Open the executor from the toolbar to batch-run all APIs in a Collection in sequence.

For the example above, if we only obtain and define the variable username in getUserInfo without executing, as long as getUserRepos runs after getUserInfo, it will likewise succeed.

The Runner in action looks like this:

But Bruno’s default behavior here is to run all requests in a collection, and although the ability to adjust the order is offered, it is only included in the paid premium version, including csv- or json-based data-driven functionality, which is also absent from the free version. It is somewhat underwhelming.

Bruno Command Line - Bruno CLI

Because the Runner feature above is limited, it is rather underwhelming and basically unusable when we want to do API automation. But Bruno’s premium features here actually only restrict triggering from the UI.

To run automation, we can also make use of the command-line functionality it provides.

This CLI program needs to be installed separately.

1

npm install -g @usebruno/cli

After installation, being able to display the version number correctly means it installed successfully, for example:

1
2

C:\qiucao>bru --version
2.1.0

By executing from the command line, we can, according to our needs, for example run the APIs in a specified directory.

The two parameters carried here - --env specifies the environment to use, and --reporter-html generates an HTML-format test report after execution completes. (For detailed parameters, refer to the documentation https://docs.usebruno.com/bru-cli/commandOptions)

The generated test report:

The above is the advanced explanation of using scripts and automated execution features in Bruno. Stay tuned for the following articles.

Reply with 大纲 to view the detailed syllabus of the QiuCao full-stack testing skills course. Reply with 进群 to join the testing discussion group and share testing techniques and exchange information with fellow testers.

item.title: The Best Postman Alternative, A Practical Tutorial on the API Testing Tool Bruno (Part I), Fundamentals
item.description:
Preface

In the previous article 【】, we introduced Bruno, an up-and-coming API testing tool that has been attracting wide attention on GitHub, offering a great alternative for those tired of Postman’s mandatory online-usage restriction.

The core strengths of Bruno, as highlighted on its official website, are as follows:

  1. A commitment to being open source and extensible, focusing exclusively on the client and never expanding the product into a “platform”.
  2. Collaboration and version management built on Git
  3. Offline use, never syncing local data 😂😂😂

In this series, we will walk through a detailed, hands-on tutorial on API interface testing using Bruno. This is the first article, focusing on the following topics:

  • Bruno installation and an overview of the interface
  • Methods for implementing typical API operations with the GitHub API
  • Environment management
  • Authentication mechanisms and encryption

Bruno Installation and Interface Overview

Installation 

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

# Mac (Homebrew)
brew install bruno

# Windows (Winget)
winget install usebruno.bruno

# Linux (Snap)
sudo snap install bruno

Using the Interface

  • Left panel: Collection management and navigation (similar to a project structure in an IDE)

  • Central area: the request editor (URL / Headers / Body configuration)

  • Right panel: response results display (content, status, assertions, etc.)

  • Toolbar: the top mainly holds some advanced feature settings (paid version) and variable management (global, environment); the bottom toolbar holds system-level settings for the tool (interface, proxy, authentication, etc.), as well as cookies and license management

  • Keyboard shortcuts:

    • Ctrl +E: environment variable settings
    • Ctrl + B: create a new request
    • Ctrl + Enter: send the request immediately

Implementing Typical HTTP API Testing (GitHub API)

Below, using the official GitHub API, we will show how to carry out typical HTTP API request testing in Bruno.

Introduction to the GitHub API

GitHub is a hosting platform for open source software projects. Because it uses Git as the sole repository format for hosting, it is named GitHub. It is also the largest code hosting platform in the world today, arguably a holy land for programmers, and jokingly known as the world’s largest same-sex dating platform

The GitHub API currently has two versions: one is the GraphQL-based V4 version, while the more commonly used one is still the earlier Restful API, whose Restful API definition has long been regarded as a model for this kind of interface.

For the detailed interface documentation, see https://docs.github.com/zh/rest?apiVersion=2022-11-28

The Time Format in GitHub

YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ

GitHub Rate Limiting Rules

To protect server load, GitHub limits request traffic. Every GitHub response header carries GitHub’s rate limit settings.

Header Parameter Meaning
X-RateLimit-Limit The maximum number of requests per hour; generally 60 for unauthenticated requests and 5000 for authenticated requests
X-RateLimit-Remaining The number of requests remaining
X-RateLimit-Reset The time when the remaining limit resets, in milliseconds
Request Parameters and Pagination

Requests can carry parameters, generally of two types: path parameters and query parameters

The GitHub API supports two pagination parameters by default:

  • page the current page number to display
  • per_page the number of results per page
GitHub Request Token

From the GitHub account settings page, add a Token configuration for accessing the API

Configuring Token Authentication

In Bruno, create a new Collection and name it github. In its Auth section, add the API token you configured earlier, and select bearer Token as the authentication method here

Besides bearer Token, Bruno also supports a variety of other authentication methods, covering basically all authentication patterns of various API interfaces.

  • AWS Sig: an authentication method for signed AWS public cloud users of Amazon
  • Basic auth: basic authentication, by entering an account and password
  • WSSE auth: Web Service security user authentication
  • Bearer Token: a security authentication token based on encrypted text
  • Digest auth: digest authentication
  • NTLM auth: Microsoft’s LAN management authentication protocol
  • Oauth 2.0: an open authorization protocol, a commonly used protocol for third-party authentication
  • API Key: an access token defined by the server itself
  • no Auth: no authentication
  • inherit: inherit the authentication from the parent level (in Bruno, a child request can use the authentication settings of its parent)

CRUD Operations in API Testing

1. GET Request — Get the Latest Release of a Specified Project

Target interface: GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/releases/latest

In Bruno, {{var}} lets you specify variables in a request, with the variables configured as follows. After clicking the send button, a response is successfully obtained.

The authentication method for this request uses inherit, inheriting the bearer token authentication configured in the collection

2. POST Request — Create an Issue

Target interface: POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues

Creating an issue corresponds to the POST method, configured in Bruno as follows,

  • Body configuration:

    1
2
3
4
5
6
7

     {
 "title": {{issue_title}},
 "body": "Found a test issue",
 "labels": [
 "bug"
 ]
 }

  • Dynamic variable injection:

    For the issue title here, we use Bruno’s built-in dynamic variable {{$timestamp}}. Bruno provides a rich set of built-in dynamic variables, which makes it extremely convenient for us to dynamically simulate request data.

    1
2
3

    # Preset title variable
vars:
 issue_title: "Test_Issue_{{$timestamp}}"

Check on GitHub, the Issue has been created

3. PATCH Request — Modify an Issue

Target interface: PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/3

Close the issue whose issue_number is 3

1
2
3

{
 "state": "closed"
}

4. DELETE Request — Delete an Issue Comment

Target interface: DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/comments/{comment_id}

Basic Test Assertions

Test Script Validation — Status Code

In Bruno, you can write Test scripts to validate results, similar to Postman

1
2
3

test("Status is 200", () => {
 expect(res.status).to.equal(200);
});
Interface Assert

For some commonly used assertions, Bruno also lets you add Assert directly in the interface to perform assertions.

The results of the above Test and Assert executions are as follows

The above is an introduction to the main basic feature usage when performing API testing with Bruno. Further advanced usage will be updated in follow-up posts. Everyone is also welcome to join the testing discussion group to continue in-depth exchanges with fellow testers. Reply with join the group to get an invitation to the group.

item.title: Browser Use - A Detailed Guide to the AI-Powered Browser Tool
item.description:
Foreword

In several of our previous articles on AI testing, we introduced methods for achieving AI-driven test automation through several different AI browser tools, including playwright-mcp, midscene.js, and magentic ui. In fact, before these constantly emerging new tools appeared, there was an AI browser-driving tool that was released even earlier (2024.11) and is likewise still being continuously refined: Browser Use. Its implementation approach provided a great deal of reference for the related tools that came later. And after more than half a year and over 40 version iterations, the current latest version is 0.2.5, and the tool’s features have become increasingly complete.

In this article, let us take a systematic look at this AI browser.

browser-use Overview

browser-use is positioned as a simple yet powerful solution that connects different AI Agents with browsers, enabling AI-based intelligent browser automation.

It is a Python-based open-source library with over 61K stars on GitHub, which shows just how much attention it has attracted.

It mainly relies on the browser-control capabilities of Playwright/Puppeteer and the reasoning and analysis capabilities of large AI models to accomplish the shift of AI from an information assistant to an assistant that helps with execution. After it, MCP became widespread, and the subsequent variety of other AI-driven browser approaches all bear traces of the browser-use solution.

How It Works

The implementation of browser-use is, in fact, an AI Agent built with Langchain and LLM (Large Language Model) that understands web page content and further generates operation instructions. At its core, the project relies on the Playwright framework to implement browser automation operations, supports multiple browsers (such as Chromium, Firefox, etc.), and can simulate real-user behaviors like clicking, typing, and navigation.

Based on AI capabilities, the system can automatically identify interactive elements on web pages (such as buttons, input fields, etc.) and, combined with an understanding of the context, generate the corresponding interaction logic, improving automation efficiency and achieving AI-based browser intelligence.

Core Architecture Analysis

browser-use achieves deep integration between the AI Agent and the browser through a layered architecture. The main roles of the different layers of its core architecture are as follows:

Agent Layer (Decision Center)

This layer is mainly responsible for task-flow orchestration and decision-making. It manages the task flow by implementing a small state machine and interacts with the LLM (such as OpenAI) to obtain decision instructions.

Controller Layer (Instruction Converter)

This layer is responsible for translating high-level decisions into concrete browser operation instructions, supporting basic actions such as DOM operations and page navigation, and also providing management of multi-tab interaction logic.

DOM Parsing Engine

This layer performs real-time parsing of web page structure and content, including providing visual recognition capabilities (OCR support), and completes the construction of the mapping relationships for operable web page elements.

Browser Interface Layer

At this layer, the browser behavior is actually driven based on the Playwright framework. In addition to the built-in headless mode control, it can also interact with the user’s browser by specifying a browser path.

Architecture Diagram

Installation and Deployment

It is recommended to use the Python package management tool uv for installation and deployment

.venv\Scripts\activate

playwright install --with-deps

from langchain_deepseek import ChatDeepSeek
from browser_use import Agent
from pydantic import SecretStr, BaseModel, ValidationError, field_validator, ConfigDict, Field
from dotenv import load_dotenv
import os
import asyncio
from typing import List,Optional
from browser_use import Controller
import json


# Unified model output definition
class PostItem(BaseModel):
 model_config = ConfigDict(extra="ignore")

 post_title: str
 post_url: str
 num_comments: int
 hours_since_post: int

 @field_validator('num_comments', 'hours_since_post', mode='before')
 def convert_numbers(cls, value):
 """Ensure numeric fields are converted to integers"""
 if isinstance(value, str) and value.isdigit():
 return int(value)
 return value or 0

class Posts(BaseModel):
 posts: list[PostItem]
 total: int

# Result parsing function
def parse_result(result: str | dict) -> Posts:
 """Safely parse result data"""
 try:
 if isinstance(result, str):
 data = json.loads(result)
 else:
 data = result

 print("Parsed data:", data)
 return Posts.model_validate(data)

 except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValidationError) as e:
 print(f"解析错误: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
 # Non-JSON format, return the result directly
 return result

controller = Controller(output_model=Posts)

load_dotenv()
api_key = os.getenv("DEEPSEEK_API_KEY")

# Initialize the model
llm=ChatDeepSeek(base_url='https://api.deepseek.com/v1', model='deepseek-reasoner', api_key=SecretStr(api_key))

async def main():
 # Create agent with the model
 agent = Agent(
 task="测试saucedemo.com网站standard_user的登录功能, 使用不同密码(secret_sauce,空密码)，登录成功则验证完成，否则需要输出错误信息。测试结果需要包含以下信息：\n1. 登录是否成功\n2. 如果登录失败，错误信息是什么\n",
 llm=llm,
 use_vision=False
 )
 history = await agent.run()
 result = history.final_result()
 parsed = parse_result(result)

 if parsed.posts:
 for post in parsed.posts:
 print('\n--------------------------------')
 print(f'Title: {post.post_title}')
 print(f'URL: {post.post_url}')
 print(f'Comments: {post.num_comments}')
 print(f'Hours since post: {post.hours_since_post}')
 else:
 print(result)

# Async main function
if __name__ == "__main__":
 try:
 asyncio.run(main())
 except Exception as e:
 print(f"程序运行时出错: {e}")

  3. Click logout (logout button not found, retry)
  4. Log out after clicking the menu
  5. Log in again with an empty password
  6. Complete the test and obtain the output result

Summary

Through the case above, we can see that Browser-Use can effectively leverage the LLM, based on the prompt we input, to decompose tasks, achieve effective parsing of the page, complete execution, and obtain results.

In terms of execution efficiency, API calls are relatively slow, and complex tasks take a long time. Moreover, once the task has started, we cannot intervene in the subsequent execution path (unless we force an interruption), which is also a key optimization direction for later tools such as Magentic UI.

But the advantage of Browser-Use is that it is already fairly mature, has good support for both local large models and a variety of online large models, has abundant community practice, and there is already considerable practice in using it to assist with test automation, including the optimization of system prompts. It is a good direction for us to leverage AI-assisted test automation.
