import pytest

def test_successful_checkout(inventory_page, checkout_page):
 inventory_page.add_product_to_cart("sauce-labs-backpack")
 checkout_page.fill_shipping_info("John", "Doe", "12345")
 checkout_page.continue_to_overview()

 overview_page = CheckoutOverviewPage(checkout_page.page)
 overview_page.finish_checkout()
 assert overview_page.get_confirmation_message() == "Thank you for your order!"

@pytest.mark.parametrize("first_name, last_name, postal_code, expected_error", [
 ("", "Doe", "12345", "Error: First Name is required"),
 ("John", "", "12345", "Error: Last Name is required"),
 ("John", "Doe", "", "Error: Postal Code is required"),
])
def test_checkout_errors(checkout_page, first_name, last_name, postal_code, expected_error):
 checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(first_name, last_name, postal_code)
 checkout_page.continue_to_overview()
 assert checkout_page.get_error_message() == expected_error

Key Points and Explanation

  1. POM Design Pattern:

    • Each page (such as the login page or the inventory page) is encapsulated as a class, with page elements and operations abstracted into methods, thereby improving code reusability and maintainability.

  2. Data-Driven Testing:

    • User data is separated from the test code and stored in a YAML file, which improves maintainability and makes it easy to add new test scenarios.

  3. Exceptional Scenario Coverage:

    • Parametrized tests verify whether different erroneous inputs (such as a locked user, a wrong password, or a missing required field) trigger the correct error prompt.

  4. Fixture Management:

    • pytest fixtures are used to manage the browser and page objects, ensuring the independence of each test case and reducing duplicate code.

  5. Playwright Auto-Waiting Mechanism:

    • Playwright’s built-in auto-waiting ensures that elements are in an interactable state before being operated on, enhancing test stability.

This solution covers both normal and exceptional business flows, ensuring automated verification of the core functional points (login, cart, checkout) and improving software quality.

Conclusion

Referring to the results given, they can be executed successfully with almost no fine-tuning, which indeed greatly improves our efficiency in automation implementation. What is most valuable is that the thinking process provided by DeepSeek is also of great reference value for the key points of our code implementation and test case design!

item.title: My Hands-On pytest and Playwright Course Is Now Live
item.description:
Preface

It has been a long time since I last updated the blog, because I have been putting together course content on hands-on Playwright testing frameworks. Now that the course is complete, I’m writing this post to introduce it (a shameless plug, haha).

The course is on the CSDN learning channel—feel free to check it out~

PyTest + PlayWright Automation Testing Framework in Action

Why Playwright?

Playwright, compared with some long-established tools, has not been around for very long: its first official release only came out in 2020, though beta versions had been available before that. Precisely because the tool is relatively new, it enjoys a late-mover advantage. Moreover, Playwright comes from Microsoft and is backed by a major company, with strong support on all fronts. As a result, among web automation testing tools it is currently gaining momentum very rapidly and is widely regarded as the new-generation automation testing tool that can replace Selenium, the long-reigning champion of traditional web automation.

Of course, the tool’s popularity is not only because it is a product of a big company; it also naturally owes much to some of its own notable and obvious strengths.

  • The Playwright development team consists of core members from another tool, Puppeteer (a web automation tool launched by Google based on Chrome). You could say Playwright is built on the foundation of Puppeteer. And Puppeteer itself was once considered one of the “three carriages” of web automation in the post-Selenium era, so Playwright can be said to stand on the shoulders of giants: it not only retains many of Puppeteer’s strengths, but also improves on some of Puppeteer’s own shortcomings, making it more complete.

  • One major limitation of Puppeteer is that it only supports the Chrome browser, whereas Playwright has built-in support for multiple mainstream browsers. Besides Chrome and Edge, it also supports Firefox and Safari, satisfying mainstream browser coverage for web automation.

  • Playwright supports implementations in different programming languages. In addition to Node.js, which Puppeteer originally supported, it also supports Java and Python, and of course Microsoft’s own .NET.

  • Playwright also supports a wider range of extended advanced features.

The Official Site’s Description of Playwright’s Advantages

  • Multi-browser, cross-platform, multi-language, and support for mobile web.

  • A resilient framework that proactively avoids many of the problems that make UI automation unstable, including features such as auto-waiting, dynamic assertions, and action tracing.

  • An architecture better matched to modern browsers, with process-level isolation that uses the concept of contexts to distinguish different test scenarios without interfering with one another. It also strengthens handling of special front-end automation cases such as Frame and shadow DOM.

  • More thorough isolation and faster execution. Playwright’s context mechanism ensures basic isolation of browser processes and millisecond-level creation speed. Its speed advantage also comes from Playwright being based on the WebSocket protocol, a long-lived, full-duplex, two-way communication protocol.

  • A variety of auxiliary tools, including automated code generation and recording, assistance with locating page elements, and powerful tracing tools.

How It Works

Playwright is an optimized product built on top of Puppeteer, and its implementation principle can be described as a synthesis of the strengths of Puppeteer and Selenium. Playwright has a built-in server module implemented on Node.js; this module connects and communicates with client programs written in various languages through the WebSocket protocol, taking advantage of WebSocket’s long-lived, bidirectional operation.

It then controls and drives Chromium-based browsers through the CDP protocol. Playwright also supports Firefox and WebKit here (in fact, Playwright itself implements a CDP protocol for these two browsers, called the CDP plus protocol here).

There is another difference: Playwright actually builds the browser versions into the tool itself, which shields away the differences caused by different browser versions.

Where Does a Test Framework Fit in the Automation Testing Tool Landscape?

When we talk about automation, we often mention test scripts, automation tools, frameworks, and platforms. So what exactly is the difference between these concepts, and where does the framework we are introducing actually sit within the overall automation testing system?

It can be summarized with the layered diagram below:

  • Script level. This is mostly about using test scripts to accomplish automation testing tasks or build testing aids. It includes test code we write in various programming languages, as well as shell and batch scripts of the operating system—all of which belong to the script level. Scripts are the direct embodiment of automation testing logic. Many record-and-playback automation tools, which convert manual operations into test scripts, also do their work at this level. It is the most fundamental part of automation testing.

  • Tool level. This layer is responsible for driving the scripts: how exactly do scripts drive program execution, and how are test actions and results judged? These are the jobs of automation testing tools. Different types of testing usually have different tools. The ones we often mention—Selenium, Appium, Postman, QTP, JMeter, and so on, including Playwright—can mainly be understood as testing tools. They can perform different types of automation testing such as Web, mobile applications, APIs, and performance.

  • Framework level. It addresses the organization of automation testing, bringing a complete set of automation test cases together. This includes case selection, control of the execution process, and aggregated presentation of results. At the framework level, the most important thing is that it supports different testing tools and can integrate different types of automation testing. Common testing frameworks such as Pytest, JUnit, and Robot Framework are all excellent automation testing frameworks. Frameworks like JUnit and Pytest began as unit-testing frameworks, and PyTest evolved by drawing on JUnit, but that does not mean their scope of application is limited to unit testing—they are equally applied to integration testing and system testing. Just as automation testing does not belong to any one specific testing phase, we should not confuse a particular testing tool or framework with a testing phase; these are concepts on two different dimensions.

  • Platform level. An automation testing platform organizes automation testing at a higher level. It needs to implement scheduling of test tasks, management of test environments, management and allocation of test assets such as test data and test scripts, and interconnection with other development processes—for example, the interconnection and integration of bug management, code management, document management, and configuration management with various other development tools.

Course Outline

This course of mine is mainly a systematic introduction combining the Pytest and Playwright tools, teaching how to build a production-ready automation testing framework, including integration with continuous integration systems.

If you’re interested, feel free to check it out—here is the link:

PyTest + PlayWright Automation Testing Framework in Action

It’s currently in the launch period with a 20% discount~~

item.title: Differences Between Testing Mobile and Desktop Applications
item.description:
There are in fact quite a few differences between the two. The main way to look at them is to start from the characteristics of the test object.

Differences in Device Processing Performance

Although the hardware performance of mobile processors, memory, and the like has improved enormously, the gap in processing performance between some low-end phones and desktop computers is still fairly noticeable. Therefore, when testing, for software on the mobile side, loading efficiency, stuttering, and similar issues need particular attention.

Fragmentation of Screen Resolutions and System Versions

Because phones are portable, their screen resolutions are limited, and with so many manufacturers and models, fragmentation is very pronounced. Therefore, in testing mobile applications, accounting for the impact of different resolutions and manufacturer customizations, and verifying how the application is presented, is also a fairly clear difference from the desktop side.

Differences in Interaction Methods

On the desktop side the main interaction methods are the keyboard and mouse, while on the mobile side they are mainly touch, multi-touch, dragging, and so on. Text input and precise on-screen tapping are more difficult than on a desktop, so in application testing these too are points of difference.

Differences in Usage Scenarios

For mobile applications, beyond the differences in usage scenarios from the desktop side, there are also some typical special scenarios:

Network Stability

Since a phone is a mobile device, network switching and unstable connections while on the move are highly likely events, so the requirements on an application’s compatibility with sustained network stability are much higher than on the desktop side.

Power Consumption

Phones run on battery power, and in mobile scenarios power usage should be more restrained, so applications themselves face higher requirements for controlling power consumption.

Network Data Usage

Although mobile data charges have dropped substantially, data still accounts for a very large share of phone bills, so controlling the factors that affect data usage — such as packet size and frequency in network interactions — is also a characteristic of mobile apps.

Application Security

Although application security issues exist on both desktop and mobile, a phone is a device carried everywhere and used very frequently in daily life, and features such as location, calls, and camera are closely tied to personal privacy. The challenges to information security are greater, so the security requirements and privacy protection for mobile applications themselves are generally stricter than on the desktop side.

Differences in Testing Tools

Mobile and desktop applications differ markedly in operating systems and development tools, and correspondingly there are clear differences in testing tools as well.

Taking automation tools as an example, on the desktop side you might have selenium, robotframework, postman, and so on, whereas on the mobile side the corresponding tools are represented by ones like Appium and airtest.

Looking broadly at the aspects above, we can see that the differences are still very pronounced and cannot be generalized.

item.title: Scrum's Four Ceremonies: The Sprint Retrospective
item.description:
In the earlier articles, we have already gone over the key points of holding the planning meeting, the daily standup, and the review meeting. In this article, we take a look at the last meeting ceremony among Scrum’s four major Agile ceremonies — the Sprint Retrospective.

The Purpose and Role of the Retrospective

Because the retrospective and the review meeting are both usually placed on the last day of the iteration and are typically scheduled back to back, many people mistakenly think the two meetings are the same Agile ceremony and treat them as one and the same.

This is in fact a misunderstanding of two distinct ceremonies — the review and the retrospective. The two meetings differ markedly in their function, purpose, and even participants, so one should not assume they are the same meeting simply because the two ceremonies are consecutive in time.

The review meeting’s main purpose is, through a demonstration of the iteration’s deliverables, to collect feedback and opinions from product stakeholders in time, so as to confirm that the phased delivery meets expectations and to make timely adjustments to subsequent iterations. Its focus is externally oriented feedback collection, aimed at the product itself.

The retrospective’s focus, by contrast, is on internal team review and summary, aimed at process and team collaboration.

So the purpose of the retrospective is, after an iteration ends, to look back and inspect how the iteration ran, drawing out experience and lessons from it.

Holding a retrospective produces the following benefits:

  • While working across multiple iterations toward the product vision, the team also regularly inspects how the iterations run, discovering problems, summarizing experience, improving in time, and steadily getting better.
  • Through the retrospective as a window, team members have a relatively formal and open platform where anyone can raise suggestions about how the team works or point out possible problems.
  • The retrospective is also an important ceremony for strengthening team cohesion, and a channel for team members to affirm one another or exchange views frankly and openly.

In short, the retrospective can be seen as a closed-door meeting within the team, a ceremony of the team’s self-renewal and self-optimization.

The Different Roles in the Retrospective

So, given the purpose above, this meeting should not be held as the same meeting as the review meeting either.

The roles that different people play in the meeting also differ:

  • Must attend: As an internal team summary meeting aimed at the team’s own improvement, the Dev Team and Scrum Master must take part.

  • Attend if possible: Although the PO is also part of the team, the PO’s responsibilities are oriented more toward the product itself, and they are basically not directly involved in product development. So when it comes to the team retrospective, the PO is not required to attend; but as an important member of the team, in many cases some opinions and improvement actions do need to be raised or joined by the PO, so the PO attends whenever possible.

  • Avoid attending: One important reason for separating the retrospective from the review meeting is precisely that, as an internal improvement meeting, some stakeholders who attend the review meeting — such as users and management — had best avoid attending, so that team members can express their views more directly. Of course, in certain special circumstances, such as major disagreements or serious risks to product goals, key stakeholders may also be invited to the retrospective. (And of course, if the boss insists on attending, it is generally hard to refuse.)

Meeting Process

The retrospective is generally recommended to be held in person as much as possible. And because the team members all know one another well and the iteration has just ended, the atmosphere should be made as relaxed as possible; preparing some small snacks and little gifts helps the meeting achieve a better effect.

The general flow of the meeting is as follows:

  1. First of all, of course, the Scrum Master facilitates the meeting. Before the retrospective begins, some preparation is usually needed. For example, collect relevant data from the iteration, such as the burn-down chart and the team’s velocity chart, as well as the current status of follow-up items from previous iterations’ retrospectives; all of this is reviewed by the team as a whole at the start of the meeting. And for relatively new teams, the rules of the retrospective also need to be explained, along with the supporting tools to be used, such as cards and voting stickers.

  2. The next segment is to collect the team’s suggestions about how the iteration ran. That is, each team member writes down their own observations of the current iteration — which aspects went well and should be kept, which aspects were not good enough and could be improved, including anyone they would like to thank individually — on stickers of different colors. Once everyone has finished writing, the stickers are placed in the corresponding areas of a prepared whiteboard. After the opinions are collected, everyone gathers in front of the whiteboard, and the SM or any member of the team reads aloud the content of each sticker card. This process is effectively the team reliving together how the iteration ran.

  3. After all the opinions have been read out, the meeting moves into the voting segment. For example, everyone may be given 3 votes, and then, among these opinions, each person votes for the 3 they think most worth taking action on in the next iteration.

  4. Once voting is done, tally the opinions with the most votes. For example, with three votes per person, the three opinions with the most votes are finally selected as the to-do items to take action on in the next iteration.

  5. After the to-do items are set, the team also jointly discusses the concrete measures for each item and decides how to carry out the improvement and enhancement.

  6. The results produced by the discussion above must be made concrete down to implementable actions, with a designated owner for each. These are to be arranged as tasks for the next iteration and added to the iteration board for task tracking.

Through the meeting process above, the goal of the team’s continuous self-renewal and improvement is achieved. A very important core here is that members should be frank and open, and that everyone truly conducts the retrospective from the starting point of improving the team itself.

Common Retrospective Tools

The main content of a retrospective is, in fact, collecting everyone’s observations of how the iteration ran and their suggested improvements. In an in-person setting this is usually represented on a whiteboard using stickers of different colors.

But nowadays many teams may be working in different locations or from home; for such online retrospectives, some online supporting tools can also be used.

The more commonly used ones include:

IdeaBoardZ

A retrospective template can be conveniently created through https://ideaboardz.com/.

Following the most basic

  • Things the team did well
  • Things worth improving
  • Actions to be taken

Collect everyone’s opinions from these aspects

Starfish

Besides the basic model above, some teams also use the Starfish to break down the observations into five different areas.

  • KEEP: Behaviors that should be kept going
  • MORE: Behaviors that should be done more
  • LESS: Behaviors that should be reduced in later iterations
  • START: Behaviors that should be started in later iterations
  • STOP: Behaviors that should be stopped in later iterations

Sailboat

Similarly, there are also models like the Sailboat, whose purpose is basically the same — all serving the goal of reviewing and inspecting, and learning from past experience for the future.

Summary

The above is a rundown of the Sprint Retrospective. In actual practice, never let the retrospective turn into a session of complaining, griping, or mutual blame. No matter how serious the problems discovered during the process are, everyone should ultimately stay grounded in the team’s development — the real purpose is for both the members and the team to improve together.

item.title: A Closer Look at Agile: The Sprint Review
item.description:
In the previous two articles, we shared the planning meeting and the daily standup among the four Agile ceremonies. In this article, we continue by introducing the Agile Sprint Review meeting, held after an Agile Sprint ends.

Purpose and Role

As a meeting held at the end of a Sprint iteration, the Sprint Review Meeting mainly embodies the Agile ideas of “customer collaboration” and “fast feedback,” and is an important expression of the Agile principle of moving in small, fast steps.

To be specific, the purpose of this meeting is to demonstrate the current Sprint’s work results to the product’s business team, users, and stakeholders, to hear their feedback on the product, and to confirm whether the current product output — the Increment — meets expectations and whether there are new opinions, so that later Sprints can be adjusted in time.

This is also a notable difference between Agile and traditional development models: within a short Sprint cycle, progress is confirmed in time with the ultimate requester through the demonstration at this meeting, rather than — as in traditional processes — waiting until a long, complete development cycle has passed before delivering the final product to users for confirmation.

So, beyond the team’s delivery of results, the more important role of this meeting is to obtain feedback from external business parties and other stakeholders through the demonstration of the product Increment, so as to allow timely adjustment.

Misconceptions

Many people regard this meeting as a delivery-confirmation meeting held inside the Sprint team with the PO, but that is actually incorrect.

It is based more on the purpose of communicating with parties outside the team.

For the same reason, under some special circumstances this meeting may be skipped for certain Sprints. For example:

  • When the Sprint’s Increment produces no obvious, directly demonstrable business change, and consists more of technical adjustments or architecture-level changes, there is little that needs confirmation from the business side.

  • When key business parties or stakeholders cannot attend and cannot match the current Sprint’s cadence. A Sprint’s end time is fairly fixed, but if key stakeholders’ schedules cannot align, the meeting may be cancelled. In that case, a later Sprint’s review meeting will include a demonstration of the current sprint’s relevant output.

  • When the team itself assesses that the Sprint Goal was not achieved and the key output falls short of expectations, it is naturally not suitable to give a product demonstration to external parties.

Attendees

Given this meeting’s purpose, a review meeting may in fact involve quite a lot of people, generally including the following roles:

  • The Scrum Team should of course all attend, including the PO, SM, and Dev Team.
  • Key stakeholders, usually the product’s sponsors (roles such as the product director / R&D director).
  • The reporting lines of team members — development manager, testing manager, UE manager, and so on.
  • Other key roles from teams associated with the Sprint’s output, such as key members of other collaborating Scrum teams (PO, SM), or functions like security, legal, quality, after-sales, pre-sales, and customer service.

The review meeting is generally held on the last day of the Sprint. Within the Scrum Team, the PO — as the communication channel with the various external stakeholders — sends out the meeting invitation before the meeting (usually 1–2 days in advance). This both informs the relevant people of the current Sprint’s main input content and scope, and helps confirm the attendees, while leaving the team some necessary preparation time for the review demonstration.

Meeting Process

On the last day of the iteration, everyone finishes the iteration work and, following the PO’s meeting invitation, takes part in the Review Meeting.

The meeting process is roughly as follows:

  1. The Scrum Master facilitates the meeting. Usually at the start they welcome the attending stakeholders and briefly introduce the participants. If a new member has joined the Scrum Team, they may also ask the new member to give a brief self-introduction. If everyone is already familiar with one another, it is just a short opening remark.

  2. Next, the PO explains the main content of the current Sprint increment, which is also the main functional scope to be demonstrated. If the Review is held only after several sprints have passed, this part usually covers the content of multiple Sprints.

  3. Then comes the demonstration segment. Generally the PO gives the demonstration and explanation themselves, because the PO is involved in the Sprint throughout and is fairly familiar with the relevant content. In practice, a team member who knows the relevant features well can also give the demonstration, and it is often the people responsible for testing who perform it. It is best not to switch frequently between different people during the demonstration.

  4. The following segment usually runs throughout the demonstration as well: feedback and communication from stakeholders on the product implementation. Based on the product’s goals and value, and including expectations for the next Sprint, they may have questions or suggestions for improvement about the product, and the team can communicate and discuss these issues directly with the stakeholders. This part actually takes up the largest share of the meeting’s time; the atmosphere may be harmonious or heated, but in the end it leads to some revisions or additions to the original requirements.

  5. So the output of the previous segment actually produces an updated PBI list, which will also be the main input for subsequent Sprints and the material the PO needs to further organize and refine after the meeting.

  6. Finally, the SM summarizes the meeting, usually recapping the discussion results, including confirming the requirements and other matters to be tracked and implemented afterwards, such as research and tackling of related technologies. Of course, this summary also serves to signal to stakeholders that the meeting is over, but for the team it is also a reminder that the retrospective will follow (the retrospective is usually held right after the review meeting).

The review meeting is generally kept within two hours (for a two-week Sprint). During the meeting the SM must control the pace and, depending on how much is being demonstrated, keep discussions that become too divergent or too deep within the time budget — for example by scheduling a separate dedicated meeting to discuss them.

Summary

So, to summarize the key points of the review meeting:

  1. First, this is a meeting held after an iteration ends to obtain feedback on the iteration’s output. It is a major expression of the Agile idea of moving in small, fast steps. But in actual practice, it is not a meeting that must be held every single Sprint. The only requirement is to avoid leaving the gap too long, so that the team retains the flexibility to make timely adjustments based on stakeholder feedback.

  2. This meeting is not an acceptance meeting; it is not used to confirm with the PO whether the Sprint Goal was achieved. Communication and feedback are the main purposes.

  3. The meeting’s process and output are an important part of Agile iteration and product evolution, and an important process for determining PBIs and correcting course in time, ensuring that the team’s work matches users’ expectations.

  4. Finally, this meeting is also the only formal window in the Sprint for the Dev Team to communicate directly with relevant stakeholders, to feel the pressure, and to face the real thoughts of users or bosses. It is of great significance for preventing the team from working in isolation, taking things for granted, or slipping into an engineer-only mindset.

The above is a rundown and summary of the key points for holding the Sprint Review Meeting. Feel free to follow Qiucao for more in-depth reviews and reflections on software development, testing, and technology.

item.title: A Closer Look at Agile: The Daily Standup
item.description:
In the previous article, we discussed the key points of running Sprint Planning, one of the four Agile ceremonies. In this article, we continue with the second of the four ceremonies — the one held most frequently, the one teams find easiest to adopt, and yet the one most likely to go off the rails: the Daily Standup.

Misconceptions about the Daily Standup

The standup is a fairly emblematic ceremony. Most teams that claim to be Agile also adopt this practice, yet when it comes to understanding the standup, there are in fact quite a few misconceptions.

  1. Many people assume the standup is a meeting owned by the Scrum Master. They understand it as a meeting like those in a traditional project, where the PM listens to the team report on their work.

But in Scrum, the SM is actually a supporting role; the team itself is the one accountable for all the concrete work. So the real Owner of the standup is the team. Although the SM usually facilitates it, the SM’s main function is to coordinate and keep the pace, while the meeting itself exists primarily to enable the team’s own internal collaboration.

  1. The second misconception is that this meeting is not a status-update meeting either. It is used neither to report progress to the SM nor to the PO. Updating status is not the purpose of the meeting; rather, the point is to give every team member a clear understanding of everyone else’s work, so as to support further collaboration during the day.

  2. There is another misconception, one that many people slip into without noticing: this meeting is not meant for solving problems either. It is simply a very brief synchronization meeting among team members. To keep the meeting efficient, avoid long discussions that dive into details. Reflecting the team’s current progress and identifying obstacles to the work is enough to achieve its purpose.

The Purpose of the Daily Standup

So, with these misconceptions cleared up, the purpose of the standup becomes fairly clear:

  1. The team itself owns the meeting. A very mature Scrum team may not even need the SM to organize and facilitate the standup.

  2. The main purpose of the meeting is to synchronize the team’s progress. Members learn about one another’s progress so that everyone knows where the team currently stands in terms of achieving the sprint goal, and what still needs to be adjusted.

  3. Finally, the standup also surfaces the main difficulties and impediments at present, making it easier to take timely action.

What Happens in the Standup

Because the standup’s main function is synchronization and collaboration, it is usually held at the start of the working day — the standup is the starting point of the team’s work for that day. The meeting typically follows a routine in which everyone gathers in front of the kanban board, and each team member takes turns answering three questions:

  • What did I accomplish yesterday?
  • What is my plan for today?
  • What difficulties have I run into, or what do I need others to collaborate with me on?

By answering these three questions, each member lets everyone else know their current progress, then works out whom they need to collaborate with that day and which issues need to be discussed as soon as possible. They state the support they need, or offer assistance when others need it.

Precisely because the standup’s function is to synchronize information, and because it is held every day, its duration should be strictly controlled and normally should not exceed 15 minutes. Everyone gives a quick update on their progress, and any issues requiring further discussion should be taken offline — discussed separately afterwards with the relevant people, going into the details or the solution in depth.

The Different Roles in the Standup

As for the three different roles in Scrum, what should each of them do when taking part in the standup, and what role should each play?

Scrum Master

As the team’s organizer and supporter, the SM’s main role in the standup is really to maintain the discipline of the standup, ensure the meeting runs efficiently, and keep it aligned with the Agile spirit.

  • When an issue arises that may need in-depth discussion, interrupt in time and move the issue into the parking lot section of the board, arranging to continue the discussion after the standup.

  • Based on the progress and work reported by team members, judge the risk to achieving the sprint goal, remind the team of any progress that may be falling behind, and coordinate other members to join in collaboration as appropriate.

  • If an impediment raised by a member cannot be resolved immediately within the team during the meeting, record it and follow up on its progress that same day.

  • Before the meeting ends, the SM can also quickly share the sprint’s current burndown chart and the status of the main items on the board with the team, so that everyone has an overall picture of the current progress.

  • Finally, the SM should keep the meeting within its time limit and end it in no more than 15 minutes.

A burndown chart is a fitted chart of the work actually completed against the ideal progress, and it intuitively shows whether the team’s current progress is on track.

Dev Team

  • Attend on time; do not be late.

  • Most important of all, of course, is synchronizing progress by clearly answering the three questions above.

  • Before the meeting, update the status of the tasks you own in time, so that the task status information on the board is accurate.

  • Any impediments, or issues that need coordination or clarification, should be raised promptly at the standup — this is, after all, the main purpose of the meeting.

PO

During the sprint, the PO’s main responsibility is to clarify and confirm requirements. But since the standup’s function is mainly to synchronize the team’s work progress, the PO is not necessarily required to attend. That said, attending is not off the table either — the PO’s participation has its value.

  • For the PO personally, taking part in the standup reveals the team’s current progress and allows a more timely and clearer judgment about whether the Sprint Goal will be met.

  • If there are questions about requirements or points needing clarification at the standup, ones that can be explained in a sentence or two can be resolved right in the meeting. For more complex ones, the PO can stay informed in time and follow up with a separate one-on-one conversation immediately afterwards.

  • Also, during the sprint, if requirements currently in progress are adjusted or their priorities change, this needs to be explained to the team at the standup in time, so the team can make the corresponding adjustments and responses.

  • Sometimes the difficulties or impediments the team identifies are related to the PO; in that case the PO can follow up promptly, including updating the team on the resolution progress of impediments that were reported earlier.

Overall, the requirements for the three roles in Scrum to attend the standup are:

  • SM - Not mandatory, but attendance is recommended.
  • Dev Team - All members must attend (including joining remotely by phone); if a member temporarily cannot attend, it is best to ask another member to speak on their behalf.
  • PO - Not required, but may attend.

Points to Note When Running It

Finally, whether the standup achieves its effect also depends on a number of points where many Agile teams’ practice tends to go off track. They are summarized below:

  • The meeting should be held at a fixed time and place. The standup runs every day, so everyone should form the habit of attending at the same fixed time and in the same fixed place each day, avoiding the time wasted on gathering people because of frequent changes.

  • Be brief. When speaking, every member should keep in mind that the meeting’s purpose is to synchronize progress, and simply explain the three related questions clearly. This is not the place to explore and solve problems. Keep each person’s speaking time to around one minute.

  • Be punctual. The standup requires all Dev Team members to take part, so that everyone clearly understands the others’ progress and can collaborate promptly on matters that need it. And because the standup is quite simple, attending on time matters all the more — no one should waste the team’s time for personal reasons.

When a member really is late, the meeting usually does not wait for everyone to arrive; the fixed start time must be strictly honored. (For team members working in different locations or remotely, they can dial in via video conference or phone, but attendance must still be ensured. If a team member goes on leave mid-sprint, they should normally entrust another member to report their progress on their behalf.)

  • Stay focused. This is a point that is easy to overlook. The reasoning is the same as above: because the standup’s function is collaboration, every member should stay focused on the meeting and make sure they clearly understand everyone’s progress. No one should be handling other work, taking phone calls, playing with their phone, or holding side conversations during the meeting.

  • Parking lot. This is a dedicated area on the board. When issues that need in-depth discussion inevitably come up at the standup, they are temporarily noted and placed in this separate area to keep the meeting efficient. The parking lot’s purpose is to prevent the meeting from slipping into deep discussion, while the relevant members can continue digging into those issues afterwards.

  • Stand-up meeting. As the name suggests, a standup is meant to be held with everyone standing. Especially for teams sharing one office, standing effectively keeps the meeting from dragging on too long; and for teams with a physical board, moving items on the board is more convenient while standing, while speaking while standing also makes it easier for everyone to hear clearly.

Summary

The standup is a routine information-synchronization ceremony during the sprint that every member attends. Efficiency therefore matters a great deal — it is an important expression of the team’s self-organization and effective collaboration. Grasping the standup’s purpose, along with the key points and considerations for each role’s participation, helps us run the standup better and truly carry forward the Agile spirit.

Follow Qiucao’s official account to stay up to date with new posts.

item.title: Scrum's Four Ceremonies: Sprint Planning
item.description:
In the Scrum agile model, the practical implementation of agility is actually accomplished mainly through the four main ceremonies defined by Scrum, that is, what we usually call the four agile ceremonies. In this article, we explore the role of the Sprint Planning meeting among the four ceremonies, as well as the key points of its practice.

The Role of the Planning Meeting

At the start of every Sprint, this Sprint Planning meeting is held first, and this meeting also marks the beginning of the Sprint.

The main role of this meeting, as its name suggests, is to formulate the plan for the current Sprint’s operation, to determine the team’s work content and work direction in the current Sprint, and to form the Sprint backlog, SBI.

Inputs to the Meeting

PBI

The most important input to the Planning meeting is the Product Backlog, PBI.

The main discussion in the meeting actually revolves mainly around the PBI, that is, extracting the backlog items jointly confirmed by the team from the PBI, bringing them into the current iteration, and forming the SBI

And the PBI used as an input to the meeting should be requirements that have already been refined and distilled together with the team. Team members should also have a full understanding of the requirements themselves and have completed estimates of the workload for the backlog items. All backlog items should also have defined priorities.

This is also the main reason why, before the Planning meeting is held, the PBI should preferably have already gone through requirement clarification and estimation in a grooming meeting, so as to improve the efficiency of the Planning meeting. Of course, during the Planning meeting there will also be further clarification and confirmation of requirements, but just to keep time under control, this part should be given as solid a foundation as possible in advance.

DOR/DOD

Another important input is the team’s collective definition of DOR and DOD, which is usually confirmed in Sprint 0. Subsequent Sprints can reuse it, and if there are revisions it is confirmed again.

Regarding DOR and DOD, we already explained them when introducing Sprint artifacts, so we will not go into detail again.

DOR is in fact the standard for pending requirements that can enter a Sprint; only requirements that meet DOR should enter the Planning discussion. DOD, on the other hand, is the standard by which each backlog item can be considered complete during the Sprint.

The Planning meeting should confirm that everyone has a shared understanding of this.

Capacity

This reflects the team’s production capacity. The capacity of team members in each Sprint is not fixed, because there may be members on leave, temporarily reassigned, or not fully dedicated to the project in the first place. Therefore, before the Planning meeting is held, the Scrum Master should gather and understand the overall Capacity of the team for the current Sprint in advance.

The Questions the Meeting Needs to Answer

In the Planning meeting, there are actually mainly three questions to answer: Why? What? How?

  • Why?

Why are we running this Sprint? The team needs to understand what value the work in this Sprint brings to the product. The PO needs to explain to everyone the value goal he hopes to achieve and be able to answer the team’s questions: why are we doing these requirements? Why should these requirements be placed in the current Sprint?

  • What? What exactly is to be done in the Sprint? If the requirements have already been refined and distilled through grooming, a lot of time will be saved here. But if the requirements have not been fully clarified, or if some new ideas arise during the meeting, the PO and the team need to work through the requirement details here, identify the relevant risks and dependencies, and reach a shared understanding.

  • How? This part is more a discussion for the development team members, namely determining exactly how the requirements brought into the Sprint will be implemented, and further breaking the requirement Stories down into different work tasks and matching them to people. The Scrum Master will work with the team to complete task assignment and balance the team’s Capacity.

Outputs of the Meeting

The most important output of the Planning meeting is, of course, the SBI, which contains all the task items that need to be completed in the current iteration.

In addition, there is another artifact we introduced earlier, the Sprint Goal. This sets out a summary of the goal that the team and the PO have jointly agreed the iteration should strive to accomplish.

Meeting Duration

Empirical data from agile organizations is 2 hours per week based on the length of the Sprint; that is, if the Sprint is 1 week, the Sprint planning meeting takes about 2 hours, while a Sprint is usually 2 weeks long, in which case the Sprint planning meeting takes 4 hours.

Of course this is only empirical data, and it will vary for different teams depending on team size, maturity, and the complexity of the work.

How Different Roles Should Participate

The Planning meeting is mainly an internal team meeting, and its participants include all team members. In a small number of cases, key stakeholders (the direct boss) may be invited; when they are needed to provide some decision-making input, they may be invited to attend. For relatively large projects where multiple Scrum teams collaborate, key engineers from other teams may also be invited to participate in some important technical assessments. But on the whole, this meeting is still mainly an internal team discussion, with participants being the PO, SM, and Dev Team.

PO

Before the planning meeting, the PO needs to complete the prioritization of the PBI and finish the grooming of requirements with the team in advance.

During the meeting, the PO mainly needs to answer the Why and What questions, propose the expected Sprint Goal, and confirm the Scope.

At the end of the meeting, the PO should confirm the meeting outputs together with the team: the Sprint Goal and the SBI.

SM

Before the meeting, the Scrum Master needs to schedule the meeting and gather the team’s committed capacity, which people need to take leave, and the time each member will invest in the Sprint.

During the meeting, the SM is responsible for facilitating, organizing the meeting process, assisting the team with task breakdown and work assignment, and ensuring that all tasks in the Scope have a corresponding owner.

During task assignment and claiming, the SM should constantly check the match between team members’ tasks and their available personal time to avoid over-commitment. This also includes coordinating on some mutually dependent tasks.

Finally, the SM is responsible for compiling the SBI and confirming the goal together with the team. There is usually also a step of collecting everyone’s confidence index about completing the Sprint goal.

After the meeting, the SM should also prepare the Sprint board, set the relevant tasks to their initial state, and send out the meeting minutes.

Dev Team

Before the meeting, team members should inform the SM of the time they will personally invest in the current iteration, participate in the PO’s grooming in advance, and fully understand the relevant requirement details in the PBI.

During the meeting, they should make sure they understand the Sprint’s goal; in addition, if any requirement needs further explanation, they should actively participate in refinement, understand the requirement, complete estimation, and proactively raise and discuss the identified risks and dependencies. Then, together with the team, they claim tasks according to their Capacity in the iteration and commit to the output).

Finally, everyone jointly confirms the Sprint goal and gives their own confidence index about the Sprint completing the goal, completing the launch of the Sprint

Meeting Process

Let us once again outline the overall process of how the meeting is conducted

After the SM convenes the meeting,

  1. The PO first explains the expected Sprint goal and the work scope of the current Sprint, and gives the relevant reasons and an explanation of the value to the product. The team discusses this part together and preliminarily determines the scope and goal

  2. Next, the requirements in the Scope are clarified one by one against DOR. For requirements that have not been groomed, refinement, clarification, and workload estimation are completed at this point. At the same time, possible risks and dependencies are identified and response measures are discussed.

These two stages are the first half of the Planning meeting, and also the PO’s home ground

  1. The second half that follows is the development team’s home ground. For the requirements already understood, tasks are further broken down and specifically assigned to people. Based on task claiming, the SM should simultaneously observe how Capacity matches up, ensuring there are no omitted tasks and no over-commitment. In this stage, depending on the situation, the PO is not required to attend; even if attending, it is mainly to answer questions about requirements that come up in the discussion.

  2. Finally, all team members jointly confirm the agreed Sprint goal and produce the SBI. This also represents the team’s commitment to the goal and scope. Finally, the whole team can give a confidence index (0~5) for successfully completing the Sprint.

Throughout the meeting, the SM is responsible for facilitating, and should control the meeting pace and pay attention to progress and time.

Summary

From the explanation above, you should be able to see that the Sprint planning meeting is a very critical meeting in agile operations:

  • Through the planning meeting, a clear Sprint goal is produced

  • Before the team officially starts the Sprint, the planning meeting enables full communication, making the overall work scope and goals transparent to all members and enhancing understanding

  • It matches the team’s capacity with the work tasks brought into the iteration as accurately as possible

  • Through breakdown and claiming, every backlog requirement has a clear owner

  • The team collectively completes the SBI and the goal, strengthening mutual cooperation and also laying the confidence for completing the iteration

item.title: How to Test Installation and Deployment
item.description:
A question I came across on Zhihu:

Could all you professional IT and testing experts tell me how environment deployment is done? Every time I just say “install the corresponding software according to the test documentation, set the environment variables, prepare the relevant materials!” I always feel my answer isn’t good enough. What is the correct answer?

As a professional tester, this answer isn’t so much bad as it is essentially equivalent to not knowing how to test.

Although this question directly asks how to do installation and deployment, it is really asking how installation and deployment should be tested. The reason it isn’t asked directly is that many beginners don’t realize that installation and deployment is actually an extremely important part of the scope of software functional testing—the person asking the question being a case in point.

The installation of a software system—especially a system delivered directly to users—can be said to be the storefront of the entire system. It is the first step in using the software, and how well it performs directly affects the user’s evaluation of the software.

So what testing considerations should be covered for software installation and deployment testing? We can look at it from the following aspects:

Fresh Installation / Full Installation

Fresh installation refers to deploying a piece of software for the first time, or redeploying it without retaining any previously installed information.

This is actually the main part of the testing, and the installation documentation mentioned by the asker also mainly addresses this part.

But there are still many test points to pay attention to when testing.

1. Installation Dependencies

Most installation programs or scripts actually have certain prerequisite dependencies:

  • Required disk space?
  • Network connectivity status?
  • Any CPU / memory requirements?
  • The version of the operating system?
  • System user permissions (does installation require OS administrator privileges?)
  • ….

Moreover, these dependencies are not only those of the installation program itself; they also include the conditions required for the software system to run properly after installation. All of these should be validated in advance by the installer at the time our program is installed. All of these are things that need to be considered and designed for during testing.

2. Functional Verification of the Installer / Script

Whether there is an installer or the setup is done by executing a script, this part is the main body of installation and deployment, and also the part emphasized in the installation and deployment documentation. Most user-facing installers actually have a graphical interface.

The verification here is actually not very different from the functional testing of ordinary software.

  • Is the descriptive information and text in the interface clear?
  • Are the prompts for various operations explicit?
  • For parts involving user interaction, verify the branches of different user choices
  • Compatibility under different screen resolutions
  • Is step backtracking provided? Can you return to the previous step after a misoperation? ….

When designing this part of the verification, it is best to work with a flowchart and map out the various different paths to confirm them one by one.

3. Installation Exception Handling

This is an important part that tests a tester’s experience.

  • Insufficient disk space?
  • Network interruption midway?
  • Local service port conflict?
  • Power loss midway? ….

4. Usability

Regarding the usability of the installer, the main consideration is whether any thought has been given to optimizing the user experience during installation.

  • For example, if you select a directory that already exists for installation, is there a prompt?
  • Is there a secondary confirmation for file overwriting?
  • During installation, is there a progress bar showing the installation progress?
  • When copying large files, does the interface show changing information so users don’t suspect the program has frozen?
  • When a conflict is detected, is the user offered suggested solutions? …..

These all actually fall into the category of usability.

5. Installation Verification

When performing installation testing, we should also understand and confirm what changes occur in the system before and after installation, and whether these changes conform to the design requirements.

  • Which program files will the installation directory contain after installation?
  • Are any files generated in the operating system’s system folders or outside the installation directory?
  • Are there any additions or modifications to the registry?
  • Are there any additions or modifications to system services?
  • Is a program group added to the Start menu?
  • Is a shortcut created on the desktop? …..

Understanding these is not only a functional check; it also helps us understand what the installer itself actually does and whether any test scenarios have been missed.

Upgrade Installation / Update

Besides fresh installation, another important scenario is system upgrade and update—that is, a version of the system already exists and needs to be upgraded on top of the existing base to the version of the current installation package.

Upgrades in turn can be divided into full upgrades and incremental upgrades.

Full Upgrade

A full upgrade completely replaces the original program files, but generally retains the existing configuration and data. The installation package usually contains all the files of the current version, so it tends to be fairly large.

Incremental Upgrade

An incremental upgrade, based on the user’s current version, has an installation package containing only some incremental program files, including script files for upgrade operations. This kind of package is generally small and the installation process is usually faster. However, the package must strictly match the user’s current version. It is typically adopted when the full installation package is very large and distributing it to users is inefficient.

Version Span

Whether full or incremental, the verification points are basically similar to those of a fresh installation. But there is one scenario specific to upgrade verification that needs special consideration: the issue of version span.

If the software has gone through many iterations and version changes, upgrading from a very old historical version to the new version often brings many problems, including the impact of changes to configuration and data structures, as well as the choice of upgrade strategy—whether to go all the way in one step or upgrade through each intermediate version. All of these can affect the testing strategy.

Data Migration

For version upgrades involving databases and changes to data structures, business data may require many data conversion operations. This is also a high-incidence area for bugs and needs to be a key focus in combination with post-upgrade business testing.

Rollback

Rollback generally refers to whether, when a problem occurs during installation, the original state can be restored so as not to affect the existing business.

This is mainly considered from several aspects:

Normal Cancellation of Installation / Deployment

Initiated voluntarily by the user, this counts as a normal rollback. In this case the installer should be able to clean up the installation files already completed, restore the original system configuration, and reset the state back to what it was before installation.

Rollback on Exceptions

Besides normal rollback initiated by the user, if some unknown exception occurs during installation that prevents it from continuing, the user needs to be notified that installation failed, and a rollback process should also be triggered to restore the system to its pre-installation state.

This is part of the exception capture and handling of our installer itself.

And even for exceptions not captured by the installer itself—such as a forced interruption by pulling the power during installation—our software should still provide some cleanup scripts to restore the deployment state to its pre-installation state. This is also one of the important scenarios of installation testing.

Rollback Effectiveness

Beyond triggering the rollback, we also need to confirm the effect of the rollback—whether the cleanup and state restoration were indeed completed correctly.

In addition, if an exception occurs during the execution of the rollback itself (as opposed to a rollback triggered by an exception), is there a corresponding solution? For example, providing a cleanup tool.

Uninstallation

Of course, where there is installation there is uninstallation. Besides verifying the installer, we also need to verify the uninstaller or uninstall script, similar to the functional verification of the installer.

Uninstallation Entry Points

Besides running the uninstaller directly, uninstalling through the operating system’s uninstall entry point is also a scenario that should be considered.

Uninstallation Leftovers

After the software is uninstalled, which files and configurations are left behind in the operating system, and do they conform to the design requirements?

Destructive Uninstallation

Create some special scenarios—for example, physically deleting certain critical files or altering critical configurations—and confirm whether uninstallation can still proceed normally.

Exceptions During Uninstallation

Various exceptional scenarios during uninstallation should likewise be considered.

  • A file is in use?
  • Network interruption?
  • Power loss? …

When an exception occurs, is there a corresponding means to handle the aftermath?

Very often, questions that look simple turn out to be far from trivial when you dig into them. Testing is an art of exploring and discovering the unknown, with subtleties of its own.

item.title: Choosing Between Testing and Development
item.description:
When asked in an interview, why did you choose to go into testing rather than development?

What Is Actually Being Asked?

The question implies that the interview is for a testing position. And the interviewer’s question really has two reasons behind it:

First, to determine whether the candidate made the choice proactively or was pushed into it.

Proactive: they have their own ideas and set their sights on a testing role from the start.

Passive: they would actually rather do development, but their programming skills are insufficient, and algorithms, design patterns, and the like are a mess.

Second, to see how well the candidate understands the core requirements of these two roles.

How Should You Respond?

Once you understand the purpose behind the question, the strategy for responding becomes clear:

First of all, of course, you should show the interviewer that you considered this role proactively. And the reason you considered it is precisely your own understanding of testing work.

For example, in one of my previous answers:

What Is the Purpose of Software Testing?

The testing role actually calls for many qualities different from development work, such as being good at questioning, paying attention to detail, and enjoying digging down to the root of things.

In Jame Bach’s discussion of the difference between testing and checking, he in fact also points out many of the special abilities that testing work requires.

Beyond that, you can also demonstrate some of the accumulation you have in testing-related areas — for instance, a solid grasp of testing tools and test automation; and if you have relevant, presentable project experience, that is all the more convincing. The implicit message here is that you did not choose against development because you lack programming ability or cannot do development, but simply because your interests lie more on the testing side.

As for the differences between these two roles, testing and development, you can also elaborate from angles such as these:

  • Development weeds through the old to bring forth the new, while testing holds that nothing can be built without first being broken.

  • Development work pursues certainty, whereas testing is grounded in uncertainty.

  • Development emphasizes creation, while testing excels at digging into unexpected side branches.

And so on…

A Note

All the above speaks of response strategies, but it is best if you genuinely lean toward this job because of the nature of testing work itself, rather than settling for it as a second choice.

item.title: The Three Core Artifacts in Agile
item.description:
In the previous installments of this series, we introduced the three main roles in Scrum. When it comes to actually implementing Scrum, there are also specific work objects or deliverables involved, and in Scrum these materials are called artifacts (Artifacts).

Artifacts

In Scrum, “artifacts” generally refers primarily to three core artifacts: the Product Backlog (PBI), the Sprint Backlog (SBI), and the Increment. But beyond these three core artifacts, there are in fact several other artifacts defined in relation to them.

In agile, artifacts serve as our work objects and deliverables. They should be jointly created and maintained by the entire Scrum Team, and they should be transparent to everyone—that is, these artifacts should be visible to everyone on the team. This is also an agile principle: it reinforces a shared understanding and communication across the team, so that everyone works on the same wavelength. Being transparent, visible, and available for reference at any time is extremely important.

Product Backlog (PBI)

The first core artifact is Product Backlog Items (PBI). A PBI is an ordered list containing all the unfinished items remaining for the product, including product requirements, unfixed bugs, technical optimizations, internal improvements, work tasks, and all kinds of product-related matters that the team needs to handle later.

PBIs should have the following important characteristics, otherwise known as the DEEP principles:

  • Detailed: detailed descriptions. Backlog items must have clear, unambiguous explanations so that team members can fully understand the necessary information about them. This is also why refinement is necessary in Scrum: the higher the priority, the more thorough the detailed description should be.
  • Emergent: emergent. The PBI is a dynamic list that can be inserted into and adjusted at any time as needed.
  • Estimated: estimated. Before a backlog item needs to be implemented, both the effort and the value to the product should be estimated. Whether these estimates are accurate is the foundation of the team’s actual productivity.
  • Prioritized: prioritized. The backlog items in a PBI should be ordered by priority; within a PBI, no two items have exactly the same priority. This is also an advantage of a list, since a list inherently has an ordering: in a PBI list, items higher up have higher priority. When the team pulls iteration tasks from the PBI, it also extracts them in order of priority.

Like other artifacts, although the PBI is also a deliverable that the team maintains together, the owner of the PBI is the PO (Product Owner). Other members do take part in adding details to the PBI, refining solutions, and the effort estimation for the PBI is also provided by the team, but ultimately only the PO is accountable for the PBI. The PO has the final say on interpretation and on prioritization.

During the creation and maintenance of the PBI, the PO usually brings as many relevant Features, Stories, and Enhancements (optimizations) as possible into the PBI as the basis for subsequent work. Then, after thorough communication with the team, typically through a product refinement meeting (grooming), the requirements are elaborated and implementation approaches are discussed. The team also breaks down concrete technical tasks and estimates the effort required.

The PBI is therefore essentially the source of Scrum agile development, playing a role comparable to the PRD, the main deliverable of the requirements breakdown phase in traditional development. The PBI is the foundation for launching a Sprint and also the source of the SBI.

Product Vision

Paired with the PBI, there is actually another supporting artifact, called in the Scrum definition the PBI’s commitment (the committed deliverable). That is the Product Vision.

The Product Vision is something that should be defined early in a product’s life. It mainly summarizes, at a high level, what goals the product aims to achieve, what purpose the thing everyone is building together is meant to serve, and what value it brings to users. In other words, it lets the whole team know what they are working for.

It is a relatively long-term description of the entire product roadmap.

Sprint Backlog (SBI)

Sprint means a short burst. It is a short, time-boxed window defined in Scrum, within which the team can complete some deliverable product features. Based on the completed features, it gathers feedback from relevant stakeholders so that the product’s evolution roadmap can be adjusted in a timely manner. It is a concrete embodiment of the agile idea of “small steps, fast runs.”

The SBI, then, is the list of all backlog items the team needs to complete within a Sprint. The SBI is therefore actually extracted from the PBI, distributed as the work the team needs to complete across different Sprints.

Usually, at the Sprint Planning meeting before a Sprint officially starts, the team jointly completes the extraction of the SBI based on the priorities of the PBI and the team’s capacity.

Once the SBI is settled at the planning meeting, it is generally kept as stable as possible. But unexpected situations always arise in reality, and agile embraces change, so a fixed SBI does not necessarily remain constant throughout the Sprint. Based on priority adjustments, and after reaching agreement with the team, the PO can add, remove, or modify items in the SBI—but the prerequisite is that the team reaches consensus.

SBI adjustments usually mean wasted effort, so within a Sprint it should be kept as stable as possible.

The figure shows the SBI already pulled into a Sprint within Jira, a commonly used agile management tool. Once the Sprint begins, the iteration board in Scrum reflects the Sprint’s progress in real time.

Sprint Goal

Similarly, paired with the SBI there is also a supporting artifact, or commitment—the Sprint Goal. This artifact is usually defined by the PO and outlines, at a high level, the core objective the entire Sprint should achieve. After being confirmed and agreed with the team, the Sprint Goal also represents the output the team as a whole commits to delivering in this cycle.

For the various stakeholders not involved in the iteration, the Sprint Goal is also a way to understand the overall progress of the current product.

Increment

Increment means increment. In agile, because of the emphasis on small steps and fast runs, the work output of each iteration is in fact oriented toward the product vision and is an enhancement on top of the existing foundation. It is not only a process of accumulation but also a process of continuously delivering value to users.

Based on agile principles, the Increment should be working software that can demonstrate the product’s value. In other words, the Increment, combined with the outputs of previous Sprints, should always be a forward-looking, minimal usable piece of software—an MVP (Minimum Viable Product)

Whether a Sprint has achieved its Sprint Goal is usually demonstrated at the Sprint Review by showing the functional results of the Increment to relevant stakeholders and obtaining their feedback.

Definition of Done (DoD)

The commitment associated with the Increment is actually the completion status of each backlog item in the SBI. So how is this “done” defined? In Scrum, that corresponds to the DoD. The DoD is a set of common definitions for the main types of backlog items.

In fact, besides the DoD there is also the DoR. The DoR defines under what conditions a backlog item can be considered ready. Only ready backlog items should be pulled into the SBI.

Other Artifacts

In addition to the three core artifacts defined in Scrum and the supporting commitment artifacts, there are also artifacts defined to reflect the status of iteration progress.

Burndown Chart

The Burndown Chart is a visual chart that reflects the progress of a Sprint in a timely manner.

X-axis: the elapsed time of the iteration Y-axis: the workload of the iteration, usually represented by the Story Points estimated in the SBI, reflecting the estimated total effort required to complete the iteration.

Based on the relationship between workload and time, first draw an ideal burndown line of Story Points that is linear, and then draw an actual burndown line based on the work actually completed each day during the iteration. How well these two lines match reflects whether the iteration is currently on track. It is a key iteration status chart that the Scrum Master and the team should keep an eye on at the daily standup.

For this reason, the Burndown Chart is usually regarded as an important artifact in Scrum.

Besides the Burndown Chart, there are in fact many other charts that can be used to analyze current iteration progress. Commonly used ones include:

Cumulative Flow Diagram

The Cumulative Flow Diagram shows the trend of overall requirements moving between different states within a Sprint, and it often plays an important role in identifying team bottlenecks and balancing the workload among members.

Velocity Chart

Another commonly used chart is Velocity. This chart tracks the work completed across multiple Sprints to observe whether the team’s productivity is stable, and thereby forms a basic judgment about the team’s maturity.

The more stable an agile team is, the more constant its output per iteration should be. If the variation fluctuates widely, it indicates that the team still has many problems in task balancing, estimation, and handling interruptions. It is an observational metric.

The above is an introduction to the artifacts—the team’s work objects and deliverables—in Scrum agile. Feel free to keep following this series; updates will continue….

item.title: Should You Tolerate a High Performer with Poor Conduct?
item.description:
What Is the Question

Will a boss tolerate an employee with poor conduct? Here, “poor conduct” can be understood as violating discipline or even the law, disregarding public order and good morals, and so on — in other words, the employee has a problem with values.

But there is actually another implicit premise here: this employee is presumably very capable (setting aside things like background — though background, of course, is itself a kind of capability). Otherwise there would be no basis for discussing whether to tolerate them at all.

The Theoretically Correct Approach

Therefore, what we are discussing here is the question of employee evaluation in management. When companies evaluate employees, they usually look at two dimensions in combination: performance and values.

The GE 9-Box Grid

For example, when GE evaluates employees, it combines these two dimensions with three levels — high, medium, and low — to produce a nine-box grid.

Green: excellent evaluation

Blue: competent or improvable

Red: should be eliminated

Moreover, in this nine-box grid, values actually carry more weight than performance: even with excellent performance, an employee still leans toward red, tending toward elimination.

Alibaba’s Five Types of Employees Model

Similarly, it is said that Alibaba also has a classification of employees into five types.

  • Stars: outstanding performance, prominent contributions, and sound values; performance resources are tilted toward them.

  • Oxen: diligent and conscientious, fully fulfilling their duties; the bedrock of the team.

  • Wolves: exceptional ability but problematic values; if they cannot be corrected in time, they must be resolutely replaced.

  • White Rabbits: appear hardworking and have good values but lack ability; if they cannot improve, they too must be eliminated.

  • Dogs: neither ability nor values are up to par; eliminate them resolutely.

So from the above we can see that mature companies have a fairly clear stance on employees with values problems: no matter how good your performance, you should still be eliminated — that is, poor conduct will not be tolerated.

Possible Real-World Scenarios

The above is more about the theoretically correct approach.

In reality, however, what choice a boss makes is usually shaped jointly by the stage the company is at and, of course, the boss’s own personal values.

Marx pointed out long ago that “capital comes into the world dripping from head to toe, from every pore, with blood and dirt.” Of course, this refers more to the stage of primitive capital accumulation, where achieving capital growth often means stopping at nothing. In other words, in the early stages of capital accumulation, poor conduct is, with very high probability, unavoidable.

So in reality, the logic behind a boss’s choice is actually quite simple:

If the company’s survival is the top priority, then delivering results and simply staying alive often matters more to the boss; in this case they will mostly be more tolerant of employees who stop at nothing yet deliver excellent performance.

But once the company has grown big and strong, continuing to tolerate misconduct may harm its health and long-term development, so naturally it can no longer be tolerated.

Of course, we should still believe that there really are entrepreneurs with a grand vision and strong character who have upheld those fine values from the very beginning. It is just that when a company faces life and death, the approach it chooses to adopt is the more convincing one.

item.title: The Importance of Communication in Team Management
item.description:
In any team, communication is in fact the core work of a manager. What we call management — turning various management methods and ideas into a team’s ability to execute — is actually accomplished through communication.

Managers need to invest a great deal of energy in team communication. Communication is the bridge and the connection, and the inevitable path to holding a team together. But communication is by no means as simple as the two parties just having a chat.

The Communication Funnel

Communication is essentially a process of transmitting information and building consensus, but in communication between people there exists a rule known as the communication funnel.

  • If what you have in mind, about the matter we want to communicate, is originally 100% of the information,

  • then after it is expressed orally or in writing, the information actually conveyed may be only 80%,

  • and the information the other party is able to receive drops to 60%,

  • even within the information received, what can be correctly understood without distortion is estimated to be only 40% left,

  • and when the relevant information is then translated into concrete action, it drops a further 20%,

  • as time passes, it may even decay to almost nothing…

So the transmission of information in fact has a marked attenuation effect, and dealing with the attenuation of this communication funnel is the core of communication management in team management.

This includes confirmation at multiple levels; checking for deviations through the definition of processes and the setting of milestones and checkpoints; and regular retrospectives to review lessons learned.

Effective Communication Model - The Johari Window

To counter this attenuation effect in communication, to ensure that both parties in a conversation can fully understand one another and reach consensus, and to improve the effectiveness of communication as much as possible on a shared foundation, there is a well-known model: the Johari Window communication model.

In this model, based on how well the two parties in communication grasp the information, it is divided into four quadrants.

  • Information that I know and you also know lies in the Open Area. In this region, the two parties share the same foundation of information, which is also the basis for building trust when we communicate; the larger this area, the less likely misunderstandings are to arise, and the more it helps us achieve efficient communication.

  • Information that I know but you do not know lies in the Hidden Area. Everyone has secrets, a real self concealed beneath the surface.
